Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do qualified University lecturers still like to be called professor, why?
Answer: It depends heavily on culture and context, and the answer is very different from country to country. In Denmark where I spent most of my time growing up and where I got my education, everyone is on fairly equal terms, and you would call your professor by their first name, and they would call you by yours. Unless it was a really old and old-fashioned professor, from back when social classes and formal social rituals were far more explicitly pronounced. Back then, most educated trades and professions had formal guild-type social structures and formal titles to go with them. Most of those titles have disappeared but medical doctors and professors are among the few professions to still retain them. I was used to the socially flat and equal cultural context when I first lectured a course, which happened in Victoria, Canada. Being uncomfortable with being called “Professor”, “Doctor” or “Sir”, I tried to get the students to call me by my first name - or any other name or nickname that they felt like using, as long as it wasn’t too rude. Many of the students were from Hong Kong, however, and felt very uncomfortable with such informality and equality, and some of the Canadian students did too. That seemed very weird and wrong to me, as if they’d been oppressed into grovelling to those who were cast as their “superiors”, and I did indeed meet a couple of colleagues there who demanded that they be called by their title or, in the case of male colleagues, by “Sir”. When I asked them why they would insist on this, they haughtily replied that “they’d earned that right”. To me, they’d just earned the right to be seen as insecure, arrogant, and unpleasant. I couldn’t respect that attitude from my colleagues but I did eventually understand why the students preferred to pay me this respect which, to me, seemed to me undue and improper. They wanted and were used to a different social contract than I was: in return for their respect, they wanted me to treat them a bit like kids and take care of them and tell them what to do. That made them feel safe and secure but it also allowed them to transfer much of their adult responsibility to me. Although I eventually understood this, it was still shocking and wrong to me and my Scandinavian/Northern European outlook: we are all just adults, and should act with independent responsibility, do good, help each other, try to improve the world, be pragmatic and honest, even if this occasionally means being rude. Now, I’m in Australia and have taught students for the last decade or so, here at UNSW Sydney. It is similar to what I experienced in Canada, with many [excellent and lovely] Asian and Australian students, many of whom prefer to pay me respect by way of titles and deference, and who often are young, far from home, and in need of some caring and pseudo-parental support. I’ve gotten used to all this, and it makes me happy to be able to teach, support, encourage and care about these students. However, I still encourage independent and critical thinking, as well as collaborating in a community of equals happily learning, creating and helping each other. Most students respond well to my propaganda and social engineering, and it very often creates lovely and enthusiastically hard-working/thinking environments. At this point, I’ve gotten used to being called “Sir” or “Professor [Britz]” or “Dr [Britz]”, especially if it helps put students at ease, but, to be honest, it still feels a bit funny and wrong to me. Some students call me “Thomas”, “Britz”, or “Britzy” or other nicknames, and that always makes me happy, since it means that they feel safe, happy and confident around me. Just don’t call me “Mr. Thomas” as a few students have done: to me, as a mathematician and a bit neurotic, that just seems wrong ;)

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Besides school, where is mathematics mainly used?
Answer: In all the best jobs and in general everyday life. We are in the middle of a job revolution where jobs require more and more high-level skills, like independent thinking, abstraction, creativity, critical thinking, clarity, and the ability to solve problems and pick up new specific skills on your own. Since those skills are exactly what (real) maths trains you to do, it is not surprising that the top-ranked jobs are overwhelmingly mathematical. That’s been true for a while now but a newer development is that actual maths is also creeping into the jobs of doctors, lawyers, jewelry makers, and countless other jobs that have traditionally been seen as non-mathematical. At the same time, jobs that require less high-level thinking are being taken over by robots and AI, and this process is speeding up. These processes are similarly happening for much of our interaction with our world and each other today: we need to be increasingly literate and numerate, and too few are both. In other words, if you want a decent job and a good life, then learn and practice maths and mathematical thinking. Unfortunately, the maths that is usually taught in school is a sad excuse for real maths education. Learning stuff off by heart and passing tests is pretty much the opposite to learning how to think - you could even call it anti-maths or negative learning. Luckily, there are plenty of resources to help you train your maths brain, for instance by having fun trying to solve maths problems at Brilliant.org, Parabola, Project Euler and elsewhere. This will make you quickly good at a lot of maths - but don’t forget the basics: arithmetic, fractions, basic algebra. If you take care of the easy basics and harder fun stuff, then you’ll quickly get good. And as a bonus, you’ll find the boring and useless school maths really easy.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What do Nordic people think of Donald Trump?
Answer: Ok, let’s see. Trump claimed that the Finns rake their forests to prevent wildfires. The Finns thought that this was the funniest thing ever, and they responded with a storm of ridiculing posts and satire videos under the hastag #RakeAmericaGreatAgain. The Swedes were far less amused when Trump kept posting belligerent Twitter messages telling Sweden and its Prime Minister to free the US rapper A$AP Rocky who was detained in Stockholm on charges of serious assault. Swedes respect law and have no respect for anyone interfering in their business. Next, it was Greenland and Denmark’s turn. Trump wanted to buy Greenland from Denmark, which is a bit like trying to buy Northern Ireland from England. Denmark doesn’t own Greenland, and these days you can’t just buy countries, citizens and all. The Greenlandic people reacted with anger and honesty, calling Trump insane, and the Danes had trouble containing their laughter. The Danish PM let slip that it was an absurd proposal, and that offended Trump who called her comments nasty. He also cancelled his planned visit to Denmark, and told the Danes that they couldn’t get away with speaking rudely to him/America like that. That only made the Danes laugh even harder, with the Danish news media joining in on the mockery of Trump. Norway, the Faroe Islands, and Iceland have so far stayed out of Trump’s way but that might soon change since the Icelandic PM reacted to Trump’s tantrum against the Danes by moving her schedule so that she would not be in the country when Trump’s man Mike Pence came to visit Iceland. A big snub like that won’t be forgotten by Trump, especially coming from a woman, so look forward to more episodes of this saga. So, what do Nordic people think of Trump? They think he’s the biggest village idiot ever. They sometimes worry about the power that this idiot has been given, and they sometimes get angry at his actions, but most of the time, he’s the best entertainment that they’ve seen in a long time. Update: Thanks a lot for the views and updates, and particularly for your awesome corrections and comments below; they have been really insightful, helpful and hilarious! ^_^ In case you might be interested, here is a related answer, this time about a little-known and fascinating (but tragic) Greenlandic incident.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Would you rather have a financially well-off husband that will give you everything you need but not enough attention or a spouse that will give you the attention you need but not enough money to support you and why?
Answer: I’ve already got an awesome girlfriend and don’t need a husband. Also, I’m boringly straight. But if I were looking for a husband, then I’d choose someone who would give me the attention I needed, rather than financial support. Why look for a partner otherwise; love and friendship and the rest is what they’re for, isn’t it? Money is what jobs are for. But that’s an easy choice for me: I am able to find jobs to support myself. It would be a very different choice if I weren’t able to, or weren’t allowed to, work so as to support myself. Then I might need to resort to less happier and more restrictive choices.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is there a way to study math when you have trouble retaining basic information relating to math?
Answer: Maths is a sprawling subject and learning to master it is a bit like learning a language, sport, music or art: there are some basics to learn, and then there’s lots of practice. With a little effort and patience, you will begin to get the hang of maths, and once you have a feeling for some maths, then you can go on to do more challenging and instructive maths. At that point, try to understand what you are doing: to be a good mathematician, you mostly need understanding, intutition/visualisation, creativity, curiosity, and persistance. You can train all of these as well. Also, like in those other disciplines, it really helps you learn if you’re having fun. So, one way to learn effectively would be to go have fun and challenge your maths-learning brain with the problems at Brilliant or at Project Euler (more coding-focused), for instance, where you can also see other users’ answers and quickly pick up a lot of understanding and tips.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is everything ultimately mathematical?
Answer: No; in fact, very little has a mathematical explanation. If you wake up and feel happy, then you would presumably not reach out for a pen and paper to mathematically work out why you were happy. In other words, maths is not very useful for explaining most things in our experience; nor is physics, chemistry or even biology for that matter. Shifting your focus away from your personal experience, mathematics becomes more useful. For instance, if we look at more than just ourselves, at a group of people, or if we look at our general behaviour, not just isolated experiences and actions, then patterns emerge that we can describe mathematically and statistically, sometimes even very simply - we are very often simple and predictable creatures. The explanations that maths gives us here are fuzzy though: uncertain averages and probabilities. Instead of looking at broader pictures, we could also look closer at things and, there, maths again begins to give useful explanations. Biology, chemistry, physics: as we look closer and closer at the small details of things, they begin to behave in very mathematically explainable ways. How useful those explanations might be is debatable though: they are good enough for us to use for creating the technology that we have today but it is still very clunky: our computer chips are literally stone age creations, silicon rock etched into tools. Mother Nature kicks our ass when it comes to tech. And when we look very closely at things, at quantum level, then uncertainty suddenly rears up again, and we can only describe a scattering of general patterns that we think that we have found and therefore call “Laws” but do not have any great predictive power; indeed, as far as we know, our putative reality is intrinsically unknowable, and certainly not mathematically deterministic. We can talk about probabilities but those do not generally provide any great sort of explanation. At a more philosophical level, we don’t know whether our realities and experiences have anything to do with mathematics, or whether mathematics is just one mental framework through which we see the world. There is sometimes fierce debate about this question. Many science-loving people point out that maths has let us perform many magics via science and technology and that maths has not yet let us down through contradictions or erratic predictive powers; therefore, maths must be universally true, everywhere and everywhen - indeed the world might be built from maths itself. Others disagree and point out the logical error here: it is too excitedly optimistic to claim that all of existence is maths-related just because we seem to have had success in understanding a tiny speck of the world through maths. That said, maths is nevertheless surprisingly useful for describing the world, ourselves and even our everyday experiences. Most people would not imagine it but if you have a little interest or training in mathematical thinking, then you can suddenly see a lot of patterns and explanations in everything around you that can allow you to see clearer and further. Maths is definitely very useful for explaining many things, just not great for explaining most things.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How does a PhD from Harvard differ from a PhD from MIT? Who seems more knowledgeable and hard worked?
Answer: The PhD degrees from Harvard and from MIT are equally excellent, partly because Harvard and MIT enjoy very close collaboration, and students from either university can study a wide range of courses at the other through their cross registration agreements. Each has its different strengths, however, with MIT being nearly unrivaled in STEM areas, and Harvard leading the pack in business, law, and humanities. They both excel in medicine and together they host the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology. Although Harvard and MIT are separate and sometimes very different in style and areas of expertise, they are nevertheless within walking distance of each other and are sometimes seen as one hugely impressive university, with greater impact than most nations. A PhD from either is usually top-tier.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is spatial visualization needed to be very good at math? What are some of the mental abilities needed to be exceptional at math?
Answer: No, not necessarily. Different types of thinking can help with different types of maths, and mathematicians each have their individual strengths of thinking. For instance, I have good spacial visualisation, pattern recognition skills and association skills. I rely heavily on these types of thinking in my mathematical research, which is mostly in areas that benefit from such thinking, such as combinatorics, graph theory, geometry and linear algebra. On the other hand, I am bad at multitasking and memorizing, and I am slow at processing small technical details. This means that I am not good at higher algebra and its many definitions and calculations, nor at the types of maths, such as topology, where visualisation quickly becomes impossible (for me at least). So, although each of these mental abilities are useful for some types of maths, they might not be necessary for all types of maths. However, there are some mental abilities that every good mathematician needs. The main one might be tenacity: not giving up, even though maths offers us many and frequent failures. You should also be curious and creative, so that you can find new ideas, applications, problems, solutions, generalisations, examples, and more. You should be good at understanding, manipulating and creating concepts abstractly, whether as spacial visualisations or otherwise. Importantly, you don’t need to be great at everything in order to be a great mathematician. Be good at collaborating and at finding good collaborators: you and they can pool your abilities and be great together.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why can't I understand why people work in high-paying jobs that have little/no altruistic impact? I.e. Finance/advertising/Business in general. (My dream job is a preschool teacher)
Answer: I feel a bit like that too, and would be miserable in a high-paying but low-contributing job. However, I do understand why people choose differently here. To me, it looks as if those choices depend on three main factors. The first factor is the set of social contracts that you feel part of. If you feel connected and part of a community that would support you when you need support but also expects you to help others, then your altruism for the community and the people in it will be high. If, on the other hand, you don’t feel that sort of support, belonging and responsibility, then it makes less sense to care about others because it is not reciprocal: you’re on your own. Many societies do not offer the sort of supporting community that would lend itself to altruism. In some of them, other social contracts might cause you to be altruistic, like the positive social status of philanthropy in the otherwise socially hostile US. In some societies, or parts of society, survival is more important than ethics. The second factor is your set of ethical values, and they can be quite arbitrary. Some might, like you or me, see helping others and improving the world as positive moral values; others see material gain as proof of their virtue, sometimes even religiously so. The third factor is the set of moral values that society around you presents to you. In most cultures these days, becoming [visibly] richer is presented as a positive value, as part of the motor of consumer-driven capitalism that most of us are part, in one way or the other. We are all highly susceptible to moral indoctrination and often act in good or bad ways only because we told to do so. Torture for entertainment, slavery, genocide, rape, and so on were seen as perfectly fine and moral by people not long ago, but societies change, and so do we, changing the societies in turn. In thirty years’ time, our present behavior and attitudes will probably be seen as semi-sociopathic too, at least if the long historical and international trend of improved morals and behavior continues. How we still mistreat poor people, women, strangers, animals, our planet: there is much to improve. To return to your question, I would not be surprised if much of finance was once again, like previously in history, seen as serious sin, and most of present advertising is hard to defend even to us. However, it is maybe more interesting to guess what other, less obvious, attitudes and behaviors of ours will be seen as evil and unacceptable a decade or two from now!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is the most boring lecture you remember having to sit through?
Answer: Thanks for a great question! It’s like asking: What is your favourite book or film? It’s a joy to try to answer but there are too many happily traumatic memories to be able to choose just one. There were my undergraduate professors who mumbled incoherently while copying scribbles onto the blackboard from their notes, never once facing us. Memorably, one professor forget to turn off his radio microphone in the break while visiting the men’s room. There were the “most boring lecture” competitions at my alma mater, Aarhus University: these were impressively boring but the lecturers were actually good, also at being boring, and we drank beer and cheered while enjoying intentional tedium. There was the predictably useless workshop on how to present your research engagingly. The main speaker told us to write a script and rehearse it over and over, just as he had, as the evidenced by his exact script shown in tiny font on PowerPoint slides behind him. This fascinating fail kept me morbidly attentive. There was the elderly gentleman who at conferences gave what seemed to be the same talk, saying no words but pointing at dusty transparencies with a stick, for endless and nearly identical special cases of mathematical sets. He is still revered in the combinatorics community for his impressively boring talks. But to be honest, I find most maths seminars too boring to endure. For years as seminar host, I would take speakers out for lunch and then sit myself in the front row of the lecture theatre. My intention was to give them emotional support during their talk but I would invariably fall asleep within the first 5min and only wake up at the sound of ending applause. (And, apparently, I snored.)

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Suppose you have very little mathematical knowledge, but an IQ of 161, how long will it take you to study mathematics full time, before you would be able to contribute on a reasonable level?
Answer: Given the mathematical nature of IQ measurements, an IQ of 161 gives you a decent foundation for studying and, with luck and persistence, contributing to mathematics. But, in the end, your chances at doing mathematical research depend even more on your motivation, persistence, creativity, initiative and independence, and on external circumstances such as choice of field, supervisors, opportunity, collaborators, luck and your life circumstances. Lots of smart and driven people study maths for years, even complete a maths PhD, before finding out that they just aren’t motivated enough, creative enough, lucky enough, or whatever, to contribute satisfactorily to mathematical research. It also depends on whether you would like a job as research mathematician - which is very difficult to get - or whether you are just interested in conducting mathematical research - which is hard but a lot easier, though the lack of affiliation to some university and the lack of academic resources can pose significant barriers to research. At the other end of the scale, if you were very driven, talented and creative, then you might not even need to do a PhD or even study for long years. You could spend a couple of years studying some mathematical area of interest in order to begin raising and answering research questions, eventually to publishable standards, especially if you could find a supervisor or mentor to help and guide you. This would not be the way to getting an education or a career but could in some cases yield a short-cut to maths research. Non-professional maths researchers, having a job but doing maths research as a side hobby, are rare but do exist and sometimes contribute great work.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: As a STEM researcher or professor, is it better to be smart or be creative?
Answer: As a STEM researcher, you need to be many things. You need to be smart, independent, hard-working, creative, honest, patient, curious, intuitive, savvy, generous, brave, and compassionate. Most importantly, you need to be tenacious and get the job done even when you have no idea how or when it seems a hopeless struggle. You need tenacity to get back on your feet when you break and fall. So, it is better to be smart or to be creative for a STEM researcher? This depends on your circumstances. If your research is to analyse many new alloys or to test many new types of potential medicines, then you need to be hardworking but not necessarily very creative. If your research area is in theoretical physics or pure maths, then you won’t need to spend endless hours in the lab but you will need to be both smart and creative. And researchers don’t work alone; we form research groups together, pooling our skills and resources. I’m very creative and intuitive but not nearly as smart or good at problem-solving as some of my research collaborators. I can see high-level concepts clearly but some of my collaborators are far better at visualising the more technical low-level details. A few of my collaborators are very good at strategic thinking and applying for grants. In turn, I am good at editing and establishing narratives for our research output. In these and other ways, we complement and support each other well. In other words, if you want to be a STEM researcher, then it doesn’t matter much whether you’re smarter than creative, or the other way around. You need to be both and you need to be many other things too; most importantly, you need to be tenacious. But beyond that, you just need to find the right research areas and the right collaborators to match your skills and traits. Good luck and enjoy!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is there such a thing as “you’re not meant to be a mathematician? I’m a graduate student that identifies as a first-generation, minority and woman in a PhD program in math. Every day I feel like I’m not good enough and a disappointment.
Answer: First of all, congratulations! Getting into the PhD program in maths is an impressive achievement that not many people could do. It’s a tough program, and usually much tougher in many ways than undergraduate studies. On the other hand, you’ve already overcome so many tough hurdles to get where you are. You will probably clear this hurdle too. It is tough though, and not fun, to feel doubt, defeat, disappointment, and just feeling really stupid and worthless, a failure. It might help to know that these feelings are normal. Just about everyone feels like this at various stages during their maths PhD program. I did, and everyone I know who studied for a maths PhD did too. It’s hard enough to learn how to find and create new maths, and you need to work semi-insanely hard, but it’s those feelings that make the PhD program so hard. As for whether you’re meant to be a mathematician, I’d say: yes, probably. You’re in the PhD program, so you’re already awesome at maths. It makes absolutely no difference that you’re a woman: recent research shows that maths doesn’t care one way or the other about that. Overall, maths skills are overall gender neutral. Of course, the same is true about your minority status. On the other hand, you do have some burdens that others don’t. You might have been persuaded by others to believe that you mightn’t be as good at maths as white men. That’s incorrect but if you have that belief at the back of your mind, then it’s fuel for self-doubt. It would also have been a lot easier if your siblings or parents had completed a PhD in maths or something similar; then you could perhaps take inspiration, direction and comfort from their successful pathways. They might also have been able to give you advice and support, and they would possible better understand your situation and the pressures that you face. You might not have the confidence of students raised to feel entitled to a PhD degree. These are all heavy burdens but you’re not alone. Do you have other PhD students to talk with these things about? Many of them will be feeling self-doubt too, and feeling the pressure. It would help you both to share these feelings and show each other support. Your supervisor should be someone whom you can talk to about these things too - and if they are not, then look for other academics to talk with. The best cure to self-doubt is time and achievement. Once you’ve achieved enough, then you’ll learn to trust that you’re ok, not a failure. Unfortunately, this cure takes years, sometimes decades, so it’s fairly useless to you right now and here. Still, try to focus on what you have already achieved, and see whether those achievements can help you think: “I’ve already cleared so many hurdles, so I can clear this next one too.” Another little but useful trick is to write down everything you do and think during your studies: every tiny piece of maths, every proof, every question and every thought. And every publication when you get those. If you gather these together in a big file, or a list, then you will quickly see that you’re actually doing something, achieving something, getting somewhere. I wish you luck and hope that you get through this tough phase!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Could aliens arrive at our planet one day with a superior technology and prove that everything we know about maths and physics is wrong?
Answer: Sure; in fact, famous “aliens” like Newton, Gauss, Cantor, Bohr, Einstein, Goedel and countless others have done this many times over. The one thing that we know with some certainty is that we know nothing with absolute certainty; in fact, the whole of our [semi]modern Science is built on that assumption: we pretend to believe what we have of results and theories right now - we could call this our local truth - but are ever searching for new ideas and evidence that can prove us wrong, so that we can gain more sophisticated “truths”. Meanwhile, alien technology is all around us but far too advanced for us to understand it: Nature and even our own bodies and minds. It’s not long ago that we discovered DNA - the hardware of life but more complicated - and it’s pretty much just this millenia that we discovered epigenetics - the software of life but much more complicated. Once-head of the Human Genome Project, Eric Lander, was entheusiastic about all the huge new advances in medicine and genetics that these new discoveries have brought but also foretold that we would not properly understand any of this technology for centuries to come. Imagine what discoveries lie in wait in such a massive treasure trove of alien technology! Big truths often emerge from little observations, like the experiments of Michelson and Morley, or even the musings of visionaries. Four centuries ago, John Dunne pointed out in a poem that we cannot build even just the smallest leaf, and we still can’t. Until we can, then there is much to learn, not only about leaf-making but about our world, reality and ourselves.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: To be a mathematician, do you have to be good in all math or just the field of math you want to go into?
Answer: You can be a top mathematician and yet only know very little outside of your areas of expertise. In fact, maths is too huge and sprawling for anyone to understand and master all of its areas. As a useful rule of thumb, it is good to be both deep and broad in your mathematical knowledge and skills: going deeply into certain areas of expertise makes you a better expert, and broadly exploring other areas of maths gives you better general overview. It is sometimes hard to balance both the depth and the breadth of your mathematical research but both are important. However, being good at maths is not enough to make you a good mathematician. You also need other qualities, like being able to search out and identify potential sources of quality research, being able to create new research, and being able to induce, visualise and manipulate abstract concepts. You also need creativity, intuition, inquisitiveness, independence, clarity of thought, tenacity, inner drive, courage, patience, collaborative skills, humility, generosity, diplomacy, tough skin, attention to detail, problem-solving skills, pattern recognition skills, … and much more. Personally, I’m good at a lot of combinatorics and other areas of discrete maths, and I’m good at thinking creatively, intuitively and abstractly, and I’m independent, inquisitive and tenacious. On the other hand, I’m know very little maths outside of discrete maths, haven’t done any calculus for two decades, and really suck at topology and abstract higher algebra. Luckily, I’ve rarely had any need to be good at those areas in my research. However, I’m also mercurial, undisciplined, and sometimes slow and dull. I can’t always rely on flashes of creative insight and abstract association: sometimes, you just have to sit down and look at the hard and tiny details of the problem at hand. I’m pretty bad at that. Happily, there is often a solution for this: collaboration. If a colleague in my area is not so creative but is very good at disciplined and detailed-oriented problem-solving, then they and I can help each other by pooling our complementary skill sets, and together get some good and happy research done. Maths does not need to be a solitary game! ^_^

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What are the problems you face when you listen to a lecture?
Answer: If I were still a school kid now, then I’d almost certainly be classified as having ADHD. Sitting in class and listening to teachers was pure agony. I couldn’t sit still and just wanted to get away. I sometimes escaped into my own thoughts or fell asleep but teachers usually wouldn’t let me do that. A few times, I managed to sleep in class with upright back and open eyes. A few other times, I sculled a few beers before class but that only made time go even slower. At uni, I slept through almost all of my lectures until I stopped going to them. Now as an academic, I avoid most seminars and conference talks if I can. However, for the first three years of my position, I was the organisor of weekly local seminars as well as co-organisor of a higher-profile joint colloquium between Sydney Uni and my own UNSW. It would be my job to find good speakers, arrange dates and venues for their talks, take them and others out to lunch, and so on. It would also be my job to sit in the first row in the auditoriums and appear interested and give moral support, and to ask good questions afterwards. Unfortunately, despite my best efforts, I invariably fell asleep after five minutes, not the best support for my speakers, especially not when occasionally snoring loudly. Although I find it harder than most to sit still in one place and be awake, I would not call my condition a disorder, and it seems really crazy that kids are given strong drugs to fight such conditions. I’m highly productive but almost never sit at a desk. It’s neither natural or healthy to sit for hours at a time, let alone being bored out of your mind in some classroom or lecture theatre. Work and learning can’t always be fun and exciting, and you need to learn discipline and how to overcome procrastination and get stuff done - but the classroom or lecture theatre or work office are not necessarily great environments for that, and many teachers and lecturers can be boring as hell. More personalised environments and better delivery methods are possible. Having to sit for hours and days and months and years is imprisonment and torture, and a waste of resources. The same is true of many (most?) white collar jobs: tragic wastes of people’s lives and contributing negatively to society and to our world.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Does God love us?
Answer: God loved humans once and maybe still does but He definitely does not like them. It's complicated so please let me explain. Long ago, God felt lonely and without purpose, so He created a small Paradise to entertain Himself. There were already other worlds and other humans but they belonged to other gods, and God has always been too socially awkward to get along with them. God now had His own Paradise but He was still lonely. He missed companionship and love, and God feels most loved when someone worships Him and tells Him how great and powerful He is. He therefore created Adam as His worshiper-friend. In hindsight, He should have gotten a dog. That would have saved Him and the rest of us (except for the poor dog) a lot of trouble. But I suppose that a dog is maybe not so great at worshiping and building fancy temples and making lavish sacrifices in His honour, not even a big dog. Now it was Adam who was lonely. God, on the other hand, was feeling happy and generous, and more worshipers are always good to have, so He created Eve. Adam and Eva were happy together, even a little too happy, and they forgot to pay God proper attention. They discovered sex and farming and thereby became mini-gods themselves, able to create new life. Instead of grateful worshiper-friends, poor God now had two tiny competitors who mostly worshiped themselves. And not only that, they were trashing His beautiful Paradise with their damned axes, fields and plows. The worst of it was that they looked so happy together, and God felt excluded and even lonelier than He had been to begin with. Poor God is not great at dealing with rejection and betrayal. That's how it often goes if you grow up as an unloved but spoiled single child. Instead of acknowledging that He was feeling hurt and sad, and managing His emotions maturely, God instead flew into a rage and punished Adam and Eve as hard as He could. They were banished from His Paradise and could now suffer all the pains of the outside world: hunger, illness, poverty, war, slavery, and death. Adam and Eve had some sons but they weren't great. They raped their mother, stole from each other, and one son eventually killed another. After a while, God's rage abated and he started to miss his humans: God is not great at coping on his own. Luckily, his humans were willing to accept his bribes and be His worshiper-friends once more. This cycle continued over the next four thousand years. To begin with, God treated his humans well, his humans thrived, and everyone was happy. His humans worshiped God and built Him great temples in which He lived in a fancy box of gold, and they sacrificed animals and other gods' humans in His honour. These were happy times. But they could never last, and His humans always became too happy, complacent, and smug, and they eventually forgot to show God gratitude, worship or even attention. Each time that happened, He again felt sad and lonely; again He felt betrayed and rejected; and again He flew into rages and struck out in His helplessness and anger. It was a toxic relationship and it often verged on complete tragedy. There were times when His humans were enslaved or eradicated by other gods' humans. And then there was that time when God just had enough of it all and drowned all his humans, except for just one family. His humans weren't exactly innocent victims in this relation either. They didn't pay God the attention and love that He needed, and there were even times during which they were unfaithful with other gods. In hindsight, God would have done well to see a therapist who could help Him with His lack of self worth and with His anger management issues. Some prophets did however help by way of couple's therapy, by improving the communication between God and his humans. Other prophets and kings gave their support as social workers and human resource administrators to design and implement a whole lot of easy-to-remember laws and rituals for the worship of God. Through such various support, God's relationship to his humans improved. They learned to pay God better attention and worship, and God learned to deal with His feelings in less abusive and more mature ways. But it was too late; by that time, the relationship was already dead. God and His humans had caused each other pain too much and too often, and even though they now coexisted in relative harmony and peace, the spark was gone. To bring their love back to life, God created Himself a Son, Jesus, who would show and tell God's humans how much He loved them. All was forgiven and the many old Laws were softened up. Everyone could join in, even the sinners and the unclean. You just needed to love God and to love each other. Poor God was really desperate and bending over backwards, on the sort of love trip only experienced by those head over heals in new love or those just realising, but not accepting, that their romantic relationship is over. God's attempts did resonate with a few of His humans but the rest simply did not love God any more, and they went so far as to unfriend and cut off communications with Him, by killing Jesus. That happened two thousand years ago, and we haven't seen any sign of God since. He probably just realised that His relationship to His humans was never great, and maybe He also realised that He is just not cut out for relationships in general. That's sad but life is sometimes sad. Funnily enough, countless humans have missed and worshiped God after he disappeared, in fact far more than those who worshiped Him when He was around to enjoy the worship. That's a bit ironic and also a bit stupid: those humans seem to have forgotten just how much God abused His humans. But, I suppose, even the most toxic relationships might be remembered through the prism of rosy nostalgia. It's lucky that God hasn't returned to try to get back together. Jesus did claim, at some point after His death, that God would one day return, but you say a lot of stuff during turbulent breakups that you don’t mean later on. As far as we know, He hasn't drunk dialed up His ex-humans, or sent them improper messages at any point during the past two thousands years, so it seems safe to say that He has moved on. Or could it be that God has found new Humans to be together with, maybe as Allah or as a small sand god on some faraway atoll in the Pacific Ocean? Wherever He is, I hope that He has finally found love, peace and happiness.

Question: How do you explain what a "vector space" is for a non-math student?
Answer: You can think of vector spaces as coordinate systems or grids or crystal structures. Grids and crystals can have many different types of shapes and symmetries but vector spaces are limited to symmetries that are straight, like straight lines and flat surfaces. Vector spaces also have even spacing, like the numbers on a ruler. The angles in vector spaces are allowed to be crooked, as in a parallelogram: its edges are still straight (and parallel) but the angles are no longer 90 degrees. Those are the main and defining properties of vector spaces, simple enough but also free enough to allow weird and wonderful geometries with many dimensions, not just two or three. What’s the purpose of vector spaces?, you might ask. One answer is that if you can show that some geometry that you’re looking at is a vector space, then you suddenly know a whole lot about that geometry because vector spaces have very strict structures and symmetries, as well as many other properties that mathematicians have shown are true for all vector spaces. You can then also describe and transform your geometry easily, in terms of coordinates and linear functions.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Since mathematically everything has a chance of happening, does it make sense that there is a chance that something is impossible?
Answer: Yes, certainly! By definition, the probability of something impossible existing is 0%. That is a perfectly fine and sensible probability. However, if you look closer at this question, then you’ll see that we can get far more answers, by noting that physics tells us that the notion of “existing” is weirder and more fractional, contradictory, putative and surreal than we can probably imagine and which we certainly will never full understand. Nothing really exists in the way that we are used to thinking of things existing, at least not when you look really closely at the very small or very big details of it all. That also means that “impossible” is too simple a notion and must be broken down into more subtle subcategories if we really want to get deep insight. Modern physics is weird and wonderful.

Question: Is it ok to ask for a recommendation letter from a professor I haven't talked to in two years?
Answer: Yes, definitely. I often get asked for letters of recommendation by students years after I have taught them. It doesn’t hurt to ask. On the other hand, the professor might have trouble immediately remembering who you are. It is therefore a good idea to send them your grades/CV and remind them, with details, of who you are and how they knew you. Giving clear and useful information will help the professor to write a clear and useful letter of recommendation.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why is having a PhD much less impressive than it used to be?
Answer: This is because there are far more people getting PhD degrees these days. In the US, for instance, there were roughly 185.000 people who achieved their PhD degree last year, in contrast to only 125.000 people who achieved theirs fifteen years ago. Half a century ago, it was only half that, about 60.000. Of course, the size of the US has grown too but taking that into account tells a similar story: in 1969, roughly 1 of 3400 people achieved their PhD degree; in 2004, it was 1 of 2400, and last year it was 1 of 1800. People are getting more high-level education these days, it would seem. However, a closer look at the numbers reveals just who those people are. Up until the early 2000s, the number of men getting their PhD degree had been declining steadily but then these numbers increased from 65.000 in 2004 to 85.000 in 2012 where it has since steadily remained. That is a big increase but is nothing compared to the dramatic rise in numbers of women who achieve their PhD degrees. Fifty years ago, virtually no women were getting high-level education in the US: 6.000, or 1 of 17.000 women. After a steady increase over the last fifty years, there are now more women achieving their PhD degrees than men in the US: last year there were 100.000 women, and just 85.000 men. The proportion of women getting their PhD degrees is in fact ten times larger than it was fifty years ago. So, women have been gaining access to higher education and have seized these opportunities. But that still only tells half the story. An even closer look at the numbers reveals that half of the PhD-achievers are international students, predominantly from Asia and India. Their numbers have also steadily climbed during the last decade or two as India, China and other Asian nations have grown richer. In other words, there are more and more people getting their PhD degrees in the US, and more women, but fewer Americans overall, and far fewer American men. That might be worrisome but it’s awesome to see that so many more people can now get top-level education. The previously high barriers to education - gender, poverty, and politics - have been significantly lowered, and that’s a really happy thing to see. On the other hand, since there is no comparable increase in academic positions, the competition for those jobs is getting fierce - but that’s another story for another time. A few random sources: U.S. higher education - number of doctoral degrees 1950-2029 | Statista Demographic history of the United States - Wikipedia PhD Study in the USA - A Guide for 2019 | FindAPhD.com

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Where and how should I publish my proof of the Riemann hypothesis?
Answer: Thanks for asking! There are several significant hurdles on the way to getting your proof published. The first and biggest is that your proof is almost certainly wrong. Solving the Riemann conjecture has defeated tens of thousands of professional mathematicians working in collaboration over the last 160 years. That you, working on your own, should succeed where they failed together is highly unlikely. It is far more likely that you have overlooked some flaw in your proof. That said, it is often possible to find some new maths that has been overlooked by everyone else, and an outsider’s fresh perspective can sometimes help. The next hurdle is that no-one will believe you even if your proof is correct. If you send your article to a research journal, then the editors will almost certainly dismiss it out of hand. As an editor myself (for instance of Parabola), I frequently receive articles from non-professional mathematicians who claim to have solved some big conjecture. Unlike many other editors, I don’t immediately dismiss these submissions - but the proofs always turn out to be wrong, and it sometimes feels like wasted time and effort to spot the inevitable errors. Next, there is the hurdle of presentation. You might be surprised to hear that mathematical research is a cultural game. It even follows fashions and trends, and I have several times had my research be rejected from top journals because it was about topics that would not be of sufficient interest to readers. That is perfectly fair and reasonable. This social bias plays an important non-cultural role too: mathematicians rely on truth, and if your topic is fashionable, then there will be more expert referees available to assess your work, which means that the journal can be more confident in the quality and integrity of its contents. This principle extends to the way in which you present the article. As a non-mathematician, you would probably write up your results in a way that stood out as rough and contrasting to professionally written maths that is beautifully written in L A T E X and following standard mathematical conventions of presentation. This would raise red flags to editors: if you are not even able to present your work professionally, then what is the chance that your maths is professional? Again, your maths might be 100% correct but editors are busy and rely on those red flags to filter away the low-quality submissions. Also, editors expect submitted articles to be in (nearly) publishable shape: rough drafts are a waste of everyone’s time. Finally, there is you. That sounds really harsh, and it is. Everyone can join the happy game of maths research, and non-professional mathematicians can contribute greatly and importantly. For instance, one of the Polymath Projects was in large part successful due to the insights of a high school maths teacher, working alongside some of the best professional mathematicians, including Terry Tao. However, mathematics is a meritocracy that cuts both ways: you can get acknowledged and applauded for your work regardless of who you are - but your work is also how you are measured. If you haven’t previously published good maths research, then editors might have biased reservations against you. That is partly fair: the likelihood of your submitted research being good is greater if you have previously demonstrated great work. But it is also unfair (and unmeritorious): your work should ideally be judged on its own, not by your previous work. That lends particularly unfair bias against PhD students and other early career researchers, and might sometimes allow renowned researchers to publish sub-par work. In your case, it is also both fair and unfair. Editors should ideally judge your work but, in reality, your lack of demonstrated quality research only adds to the pile of red flags that those busy editors will see raised. I am sorry if this all sounds daunting and depressing to read - but please don’t give up! One way to see this in a positive light is that you are striving towards perhaps the greatest goal that maths presently taunts us with. Such a great achievement deserves equally great effort, and a few cultural and presentational hurdles are nothing compared to having solved the Conjecture. And knowing what those hurdles are might help overcome them. So what can you do right now? You should check your proof again, this time with the assumption that it is wrong. Try to break it as hard as you can, leaving no tiny detail or explanation unturned. If your proof survives, then learn L A T E X (it’s worth learning anyway!) and look up mathematical research articles on the Riemann hypothesis to try to emulate the style and quality of those articles. Then, having made a decent draft, try to find a professional expert on the Riemann Hypothesis who might be willing to assess your proof and give you detailed advice on how to proceed. Good luck!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How true is it that everyone is either a math or an English person, but never both? Why?
Answer: No; you can be good at both. There are several reasons for why maths and language skills are seen to be mutually exclusive. One reason is that school subjects and classes get easier to administrate if you divide subjects into big and clunky categories, like Art, Science, Humanities or whatever. That is useful but makes it harder for students to choose subjects freely and broadly, and it gives the wrong impression that these categories are segregated. Another reason is cultural: these days, Western culture often sees maths and STEM subjects as [unpopularly/trendy] nerdy, rational, logical, “linear thinking”, and in contrast to the [popularly/trendy] “human”, “creative”, “emotional”, “social” subjects, which language is seen to below to. This cultural view is wrong: maths is also creative and emotional, and language is also rule-bound - but you might not get to do much creative and happy maths in school; that often comes later, partly due to bad curricula and teachers, and overemphasis on assessments. In other cultures and in the past, maths and language were seen as far more overlapping than they are in the West today: think of classical Greek poetry and its strict mathematical patterns, for instance.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What would you advise a student who feels he already has a higher level of critical thinking, or even IQ, than most of his professors?
Answer: I’ve taught and mentored countless students who are brighter than me, and it’s always a joy and privilege. They are often excited about topics that are of interest to me, and they often have excellent ideas and insights, so I’ve enjoyed many excellent discussions with them. Whenever possible, I invite them to do research with me, and that has sometimes led to collaboration. These students have always been polite, and although they are smarter than me, they have also always recognised that I have experience and insight that might be of use to them: being bright, having excellent critical and creative thinking, and having some great new ideas is only part of what it takes to do research and get it published. In turn, these students bring out some paternal instinct in me, and I feel like helping and supporting them to become mature, successful and happy researchers. So, my advice to her or him is usually: “Welcome, and feel free to drop by and chat/email anytime! :) ”.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How much does a student depend on a good professor/teacher?
Answer: Put it this way: most students can learn a course and complete a degree despite bad teachers — but a good teacher can inspire you to find your path of passion and to grow as a person. That’s better than just learning; that’s invaluable. I was lucky to have an awesome maths teacher in my last three years of high school, Ivan Tafteberg Jensen. Although he was an excellent teacher, I didn’t benefit much from his lessons since I slept through half of them: those years were hectic, chaotic and sleep-deprived for me. What I did benefit from was his scholarly manner, going far beyond curriculum to invite us to investigate and discover maths, and from trying to live up to his high expectations. I still remember the nervous but proud joy of going to the blackboard to solve challenging proof questions that he posed, and I remember equally vividly the disappointment in myself when I failed to answer some question that he visibly hoped that we might answer. More than anything, I remember the open-ended, non-assessed maths research projects that he gave us, where we would spend a week or two just doing research on some topic, paired up with a classmate, with some carefully designed prompts and hints to get us started in the right direction. For my final maths project from that class, I had a week to study and write up a 15-page report on spherical geometry. Looking back at it, I’m impressed by how many good theorems I managed to find in that week which weren’t in the textbooks, and to find errors in those textbooks too. This was the sort of joyous and creative research-thinking in maths that I would not get to do before studying my PhD. Just before I graduated from uni, I met my high teacher by coincidence and told him about my PhD topic. It turned out that he had written a maths PhD thesis in almost exactly the same research area. Was my choice of PhD topic in some way influenced by him and his inspired love for those areas of maths? I don’t know - but I do know that he made me hungry and keen to do more research in maths. Now, I am a lecturer myself, no longer a student. And yet I still benefit from Ivan as well as from my later teachers and supervisors Gian-Carlo Rota, Peter Cameron and Carsten Thomassen, all giants in mathematical research and all tremendously kind, generous and inspiring people. Their shining examples as researchers, teachers and as people has taught me many valuable lessons, and my memories of them continue to help me become a better teacher, supervisor and mentor. I know that I make a big difference to many of my own students, which is always a great joy to see, and it’s an even greater joy to see my students experience the joys of discovering maths and helping others to do so too. Many of these awesome students have themselves become fantastic and inspiring teachers; and so it continues, like ripples expanding outwards, spreading joy and generosity for mathematical discovery.
