Question: How can I better understand a Cartesian product? How can you explain it in a simple way?
Answer: You can think of the Cartesian product A × B of two sets A and B as the set of points in the (Cartesian) coordinate system with A on the one axis and B on the other. For instance, if A is the set { 1 , 2 , 3 } and B is the set { a , b } , then the coordinate system would look like this: There are six points in this coordinate system, such as the point ( 3 , b ) . The Cartesian product A × B is the set of all six of these points: A × B = { ( 1 , a ) , ( 2 , a ) , ( 3 , a ) , ( 1 , b ) , ( 2 , b ) , ( 3 , b ) }

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How often do you see your brightest students fail?
Answer: I’ve seen this more often that you might expect. It’s not easy to be a student and most of my students struggle with uncertainty, expectations, loneliness, and despair. Many of my (maths) students tell me that they feel really stupid and think that there must be something wrong with them, since others in their class just seem to get everything straight away. What I tell these students is that every student feels this way but that some are better at hiding it than others. I tell them that the very brightest students tell me that they feel too stupid too, that the other very brightest students are just that bit brighter. Hearing this makes most students feel better. But the very brightest students rarely feel better since their main nemesis is their own high expectations. Some want to be the best of the best, or to feel gifted and special, or the get praise and admiration from everyone. That’s increasingly hard to achieve if you find yourself in classes together with all the other winners of that game. This forces some students to painfully re-evaluate their self-image and their motivation for studying. Winning is no longer a viable reason for working so hard. Others just need to be perfect at what they do, and any tiny error means total failure. Some of my super-bright students dropped out because they only get 98% averages. And yet others crumble beneath their heavy work loads and even heavier expectations that have been imposed on them, by parents or supervisors or scholarship-giving governments. Years of pushing yourself hard without pause takes its toll. And finally, there’s alienation. The very brightest students often feel lonely and misunderstood since their burdens are heavier than most students, and yet other students think that these bright students have it easy. These days, I give these brightest students extra care and support, encouraging them when they do well but also letting them know that it’s going to be ok even if they fail now and then or if they just need a break.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What are the disadvantages of scientific invention?
Answer: This is a great question to which many answers could be given. For instance, one could look at how the scientific invention, and scientific thinking more generally, incurs loss of certainty. If you prefer belief, tradition, or culture over observation or thinking as your source of truth, then science is not to your advantage. Or, for instance, one could look at how scientific invention can cause severe social and ecological disruption, not always to advantage; examples are almost too many to think of. Topical ones right now include plastic and fossil fuel energy, and how they used to be to our advantage but are now to our great disadvantage. To me, a more interesting disadvantage of scientific inventions is that they are initially our servants but often end up as our masters, due to our own psychology. Think, for instance, of the “modern” agricultural farming revolution that happened thousands of years ago in many places around the world [ignoring here much older and more casual farming practices]. Farming, in this modern sense, is hard work for little gain if your population is tiny and your natural resources abundant. In colder areas, however, the hard work was worth it in order to have insurance against harsh winters. However, once people were used to the longer working hours and were able to produce more food, then they got greedy and ate up the efficiency gain, and multiplied. Each new scientific invention for producing food more effectively has led populations to grow larger and more dependent on these inventions, so we are now trapped and cannot return to what we once were, at least not without great disruption and pain. I would guess that most scientific inventions that seem, at the time, to improve our lives, either by efficiency gains or by making us more comfortable, ensnare us like this: if we have the chance to take more, then we often will, and then end up relying on having more. Despite our many scientific advances and the efficiency gains that we keep achieving, we spend more effort on work than our distant ancestors did. This might seem contradictory and, indeed, it is a phenomenon described as the Jevons Paradox. We often choose short-sighted greed over long-term benefit; an icon for this way of thinking is the monkey trap: once we achieve something, we would rather keep holding on to it, even if it is to our longer-term disadvantage. Further disadvantages to many of our scientific “improvements” are that we are often happy - or unaware - to pay significant costs for them. Think again of modern farming: it might have granted us food security but it has often come at the cost of lower food quality and variation and, of course, damage to both health and environment. Ironically, the farming that made our food supplies more secure have later led to greater risk exposure, illustrated for instance by the Great Famine which devastated Ireland when depended-on potato crops became infected and died. As something to think about, you might like to think of other big scientific inventions that have trapped us, in the sense that they incur us great cost or would demand from us a heavily toll to give up. The examples are many, so a perhaps harder challenge is in order: can you think of any scientific inventions that have come without any long-term cost of any kind?

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What are the book-keeping skills or advice you would like to share with a new PhD student?
Answer: Take notes of everything, somewhere, somehow: your thesis outlines, aim, timelines, progress; your supervisor’s comments, questions, advice; research article/book/database citations, descriptions, categorisations (and download/scan those articles and books to put in a folder for quick and easy reference!); seminar abstracts, and more. But most importantly: your own aims, ideas, questions, comments, hypotheses, results, random musings, even doodles (they can later help you remember where some important note is found). This all seems obvious but most people don’t take and keep accessible notes. And unless you are one of the few people with perfect memory recall, then it is almost certain that you will forget something important, no matter how exciting and unforgettable it seemed at the time. Just to illustrate just how bad our (well, my) memory is, here is a funny little - and true - story. Some years ago, I was browsing through random articles in my field, not paying much attention, when one article caught my attention. Its results were elegant and highly relevant to my research, and the article was beautifully written. Intrigued, I looked to see who the author was. It was me. I’d just forgotten about those results and those ideas, after only a couple of years. (Poor memory aside, it was nice to see that article had at least one appreciative reader, even it if was only myself ;) ) So yeah: takes notes!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Can you give a cool real world application of math, that gave you an advantage over other people?
Answer: Thanks for asking! I’m a mathematician mostly working in pure maths, especially in combinatorics, graph theory and related areas. A lot of my research is awesome fun and has good long-term value but is also hard and esoteric, has little immediate impact, and holds even less interest to most people. That’s why I sometimes take a break from the pure maths to work on applied projects where I can offer mathematical expertise to help non-maths researchers. These projects are always fun and interesting. They might involve a lot of work but rarely involve much hard thinking, and the short-term impact and attention is always greater than my pure maths research. Sometimes, these applied projects are with other academics; and sometimes I consult for industry and government. Here are some of the projects so far: Some of these projects involved surprisingly hard maths, like the chocolate machine project. But most of the time, I’ve found that you don’t need deep maths in order to be able to give real mathematical help to other researchers or to industry or government: 1st or 2nd-year undergraduate maths is often enough, sometimes even just high school maths. The people you’re helping might even know the maths themselves - but they might not know which maths to use, and they might not have the confidence to trust their own mathematical abilities. In fact, your advantage as a mathematician in solving real-life problems is often just your ability to think clearly and abstractly about a problem. About a decade ago, I was asked to help ANSTO, Australia’s only nuclear facility, with a problem. Twice a year, they had to suffer three weeks of interrupted operations so that an expensive US nuclear expert could fly in to check and calibrate their equipment and the many sensors. They wanted to ask their boss, the Australian minister in charge of nuclear issues, for permission to cut down these checks to just once every 1.5 year, and they wanted me to use their sensor data to statistically conclude that it would be safe to do this. I remember our meetings: they included one of the bosses of ANSTO as well as their impressive chief engineer who had been in charge of building the whole facility some years back. These were top experts in their fields, and I knew just about nothing about their work and areas of expertise. Nevertheless, as a mathematician - and as someone with an outsider’s perspective - you can often see things that might be hidden to others. Here, it was immediately clear to me that you can’t ask your minister to reduce the safety of your nuclear facility to a third. That would not go well, and might even lead to embarrassment, even if my report could somehow convince that such safety reductions were statistically prudent. This nuclear facility is very small (20MW, or 1/300th the size of the biggest reactors), so even if something went wrong, then you would still only see a pretty aqua-coloured well of water, now maybe a slightly different shade of blue. Even so, a small nuclear facility is still nuclear and therefore highly sensitive, politically speaking. Luckily, I could give them useful advice: do like in the US (seen by minister as having gold standards), and invest in real-time sensor monitoring. By doing that, ANSTO could brag about being up to date with modern and improved security, and since the improved security would actually eliminate the need for many disruptive and expensive expert inspections, ANSTO could soon make their case to skip those. I’m not sure what happened after this because I’d talked myself out of a job here, but better to give good advice for free than to get paid to do damage. In any case, it was cool and interesting to see how a little maths training, as is often the case, lets you see further than even experts in their own field.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is the best age to be as an adult?
Answer: The answer is surprisingly clear: as an average person (in most not-poor countries), you are fairly and increasingly happy up to roughly 20–25 years of age, and then ok happy but possibly less happy until your turn 35 or so. But then your happiness crashes and burns steadily until you are 55 or so, after which you again can count (on average) on getting steadily happier. There are many cultural and historical factors to take into account here, but the trends are aligned, at least in most non-poor countries: kids are increasingly happy, as their skills, social value and independence grow, but then responsibilities hit, and life gets heavy. Worse still, you then achieve your goals and dreams, and then you lose purpose and hope, and face the existential crisis of wondering what all the effort was for. At that point, you probably have kids and a frayed romantic relationship, and a responsibility-heavy job, and you’re maybe [feeling?] less physically attractive, and your close friends might be off the radar with their own problems. And so on. It’s a tough time, and often a shit time, though you might notice an increase in influence and power due to your experience and possible expertise and leadership. In any case, the statistics are clear: from your first real mid-life crisis around the 35 year mark or so, there is a dismal desert until you’re actually and reliably happy again, around the 55–60 year mark. Of course, you might buck the trend, or be really happy now and then in the interim, but these are the average stats. However, after that long downturn, however, you are less burdened by the stresses, aims, and responsibilities of your early years, and you can then look forward to a steady and even linearly upwards line of happiness. Looking at life as a whole, your adult life is best when you are 80 or older. That’s a long time to wait, so it might be worth highlighting the early happiness of youth: up till 25 or so. Enjoy youth, if possible. But life is also good between 55 and 80. Of course, all of these numbers are averages, and although they are fairly precise averages, they don’t necessarily reflect your particular circumstances. This was all statistics and general life advice. Let’s supplement this with a-personal and realist angle: I would have to say that life is best at my exact age (45) right now, or at least within a year ago, and the best time of life might be right now too. Life has been a wild roller coaster of ups and down and unexpected sideways adventures, and I often feel quite worn out and frazzles by the twists and turns. But it’s also been a life full of purpose, love, loss, achievement, failure, adventure, interest, despair, depression, hope, success, and much more. In the hindsight of memory, happiness, loss and so much more, what in life was good and what was bad? It’s very hard to tell, and most experiences and actions have been both. I try to do and be good but often fail, and I try to experience my life as good, but things are more complicated - and more interesting and beautiful - than what we can see through the topics of simple best/worst metrics. Do your best, enjoy life, both the pain and the pleasure, and don’t expect your life to turn out as you expect it to. But it’s not all chaos and fate either: you can do your part, and you don’t need to be an asshole. Act with goodwill and humility, towards those around you and those around the world. That might make you (and others) happy, also in the long term.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Has every college math professor discovered at least one new theorem?
Answer: Not every maths professor, but most have. In order to get the job as maths professor, you usually need a maths PhD, and in order to get a maths PhD degree, you need to complete research that results in theorems that are new and significant.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How do some professors give lectures without any notes/index cards at the time of the lecture?
Answer: We know the subject; we designed and created the lecture; and we prepare each time before giving it. If I prepare for a lecture and find that some detail, or the overall narrative, is a bit fuzzy to me, or if some explanation might sound fuzzy to my students, or if the emotional notes struck sound a bit off, then I think about the problem and modify what needs to be changed, until it works. Over time, most narratives, details, and conveyed emotions, become second nature to you, and you can eventually give a lecture on the fly without preparation, let alone notes.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is mathematical research more challenging than theoretical physics research for someone with an undergraduate degree in either field?
Answer: No. Whether you find maths research more or less challenging than research in theoretical physics really just depends on where your talents, experience and interests lie. This is because theoretical physics is often very mathematical, to the extent that some fields of maths and theoretical physics become one and the same. Some of my own research lies within such overlaps (about Tutte polynomials). I have colleagues who are expert researchers in theoretical physics who find my mathematical areas of research very challenging, and I find their areas of research just as challenging, even though both areas are essentially mathematical. The same is true of many of my mathematical colleagues who find my research areas challenging, just as I find their research areas challenging. So, if you are thinking of whether to pursue research in theoretical physics or in mathematics, the best thing to do is to pursue the research areas that are of greatest interest to you, regardless of whether they might be classified as maths or as physics. Best of luck, and enjoy! :)

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: As a student, has your teacher or professor ever suggested that you are unintelligent or in anyway undermined your self confidence and potential for future success? Do you think it was intentional and how did it impact you?
Answer: I experienced this many years ago, and it had a big negative impact on me. I was 13 and my family had recently moved to Denmark from Australia. We had lived in Denmark some years earlier, when I was 4–8 years old, and I’d become natively fluent in Danish. But, during the next three years in Australia, I had somehow completely forgotten all of my Danish, and I’ve never since been able relearn it 100% as a native speaker. So, when I began to have cooking classes at school, I was still relearning basic Danish, and still had limited vocabulary. Unfortunately, cooking involves countless special words for all the kitchen tools and cooking methods. If you were learning English, then words like “simmer”, “saute”, “blanche”, “casserole”, “skillet” would be incomprehensible, and so it was for me in those Danish school cooking classes. Our cooking teacher was this very old, tough and nice lady who was an excellent cook and not a bad teacher. Unfortunately, she had no patience for my slow incomprehension and told me off in every class. Those two years of cooking failures were traumatic for me, and it was almost a relief when my teacher gave up on me. While my classmates were cooking, I was to clean up and wash towels, which was embarrassing but at least I wasn’t getting told off anymore. This experience really shouldn’t have made any difference to my life but it did. For the next twenty years, I was convinced that I was a terrible cook, and I had panic attacks at the thought of cooking meals for guests. And fears can be self-fulfilling: I was a pretty pathetic cook. Happily, life later served up bigger traumas to deal with, and lots of old fears dropped away, including this one. I learned to cook well and now love cooking. If this tiny period of undermining could have such a big impact on me, then think of just how big the impact would be if you were told from an early age that you were stupid or at least less suited to studies than others? This is what happens to most students with respect to maths; no wonder maths is feared and hated by so many students! Culture keeps telling us that maths is very hard, that you are stupid at maths and won’t be able to learn. This message is so strong and pervasive that we, its victims, believe and internalise it, and self-sabotage by giving up on learning maths. As co-supportive victims, people band together to oppose what is hurting them, which in this case is maths. That makes maths not only scary but also unpopular, making it even less accessible to students. And, if you’re a girl, then you’re fed this toxic message in double doses: girls can’t do maths as well as boys, and it’s not a girl thing to even be interested in maths. But that message is completely wrong. Maths might be harder than most subjects but that doesn’t mean that you can’t learn it. And it doesn’t mean that you can’t be good at it and even enjoy maths. I’ve taught countless students who were panicky scared of maths, convinced that they were too stupid to ever understand it. But, with support and patience, my colleagues and I have been able to show many of these students that they can indeed learn maths and even be really good at it; that they are actually really smart. It’s a beautiful thing to see people realise their own worth, realise that they are smart, and no longer be scared but instead be excited about their learning and thinking. One negative comment can make you lose your confidence for years. But you can regain it again, especially by achieving enough small successes to convince even you that you’re bright enough, good enough. So please don’t give up even if you have lost your confidence! And, teachers: please never ever tell any student that they’re stupid!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Does God exist?
Answer: This is one of my favorite questions. My answers include: 1) Sure, I’ve met Her! 2) Of course not! 3) Not any longer. 4) Yes. I’ve written about 2) and 3) here and here. So I’ll now tell you a story to explain 1) and 4). A couple of years ago, my life and I were quickly falling off the rails. I felt deeply depressed, unloved and surrounded by ever-growing hostile chaos. My only escape was my stressful but happy work and the beach by which I lived. There, I climbed the dangerous cliffs and jumped into sea, especially during the big thunder storms when waves were big and rough. I wasn’t really trying to die or get hurt but the danger, cuts and bruises made me feel alive and happy, if just for a while. It was during one particularly rough night of swimming in thunder storm seas that I met God. To be completely truthful, I met Mother Ocean. Jumping in the waves, I’d learned that it’s best to dive under or into the wave swirls, and submit to their rhythm, not fight it. This night, I submitted completely to the roll of the waves and just let myself relax and go limp. That was when, in the middle of being tumbled around underwater, everything suddenly became silent and translucent, and I felt this huge and divine presence all around me. It felt like being embraced like a baby by a loving if somewhat rough and clumsy mother. All my sadness and loneliness fled, and I was filled with love and so much happiness that I started to cry even while still underwater. I had this experience several times afterwards, in the weeks to follow, though not as intensely as the first time. At the time, I didn’t believe in any god but here was Mother Ocean Herself, or at least a minuscule part of Her, to give me Her love. For months after that, I was full of gratitude towards Her, and I always greeted and thanked Her happily whenever I saw Her. I sometimes still do. Of course, there is not really an ocean god, no Mother Ocean. But, then again, She exists. These two truths aren’t contradictions; they are just truthful in two different ways. At the time, I needed Her to exist, and so She did, at least in my mind. Now that I have gotten back on my feet, I don’t need to believe in Her, and so She no longer exists. It is sometimes good and healthy to believe in inner truths that we know are untrue on the outside, like believing that I’m lying down at rest right now, not spinning around at unimaginable speeds through space, which is the actual truth. Sometimes, you might create God or some other untruth when you really need help. But at other times, it’s healthier to face facts, so that you don’t ignore that overdue bill or that massive mess that you’ve made. Once your untrue inner truth has helped you get back on your feet, it’s time to pull yourself together and act like a responsible adult, banish your gods, and face the world as it is. And it tends to be even more beautiful and divine than our inner visions, as long as we have the strength and clarity to see.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Should you apologize for sending an email to a professor after midnight?
Answer: No; certainly not. Professors receive - and often check - emails around the clock, from all over the world: academic work is an international pursuit. Given how busy professors are, they are used to managing time and tasks, so don’t necessarily expect an immediate reply. But the positive flip side to that coin is that you don’t need to worry about sending emails to professors outside of what in other professions would be considered normal work hours.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do professors care if students are interested in the lecture?
Answer: Some of my courses are elective, meaning that students will generally choose them because they are interested in the course contents or because they have heard good things about the course. Other courses, like basic 1st year linear algebra, are compulsory courses for several hundreds of students who have no interest in maths, and often hate maths, but need to learn it in order to learn physics, or engineering or biology, for instance. Sometimes, I get to teach postgraduate courses which cater to highly talented and motivated maths students. I don’t care whether any of these students are interested in the course content to begin with, but it is my privilege and personal challenge to try to entice every student to enjoy the lectures and become interested and engaged with the mathematics presented there. That’s a fun challenge, and a different one for each level of students. It’s a joy to see students who hated maths suddenly see it differently and as something that they can relate to. It’s a different sort of joy to make a course live up to and go beyond expectations of those students who were looking forward to it. These challenges are a big part of why I love teaching.
